title: Farid: the Creator in creation
hook: the Creator lives in creation and creation in the Creator, so whom can we call bad (Farid salok, ang 1381)
tomorrow: Farid: the crows and the eyes

segments.voice: Yesterday, Farid on the blow you don't return. Your line was go home in peace. Did you leave one slight outside the door? Today, Farid gives the reason underneath it. Day two hundred sixty.

Anyone who's spent time around small children has heard the rule, or used it. Not: you're a bad boy. Instead: that was a bad thing to do. Teachers and parents swear by it, because a child who keeps hearing he is bad starts to believe it. Grown-ups break that rule about each other all day, mostly in their heads: that coworker is useless, that cousin is impossible. And once someone's filed under bad, you stop seeing anything else in them. Sheikh Farid, the Sufi of Pakpattan, asked a question that makes that filing system very hard to keep running. Today, Farid: the Creator in creation.
screen: `NOT: YOU'RE A BAD KID.` → `THAT WAS A BAD THING TO DO.` → `FARID'S QUESTION.`

segments.voice: On Ang 1381 comes this salok: fareedaa khaalak khalak mahi khalak vasai rab maahi; mandaa kis no aakheeai jaa tis bin koee naahi. Farid, the Creator is in the creation, and the creation lives in God. Whom, then, can we call bad, when there's no one without Him? If the first half sounds familiar, it should. Six days ago, Kabir's hymn on Ang 1349 used the very same pair of Arabic words: khaalik, the Creator, and khalak, the creation, each folded into the other. So today isn't a new idea so much as an older voice. Farid lived in the thirteenth century, about two hundred years before Kabir, and the Gurus kept both in one book. But Farid's question is narrower, and sharper. Kabir asked who is good and who is bad. Listen to Farid's verb: aakheeai, to call, to say out loud. Not who is bad, but whom shall we call bad. It's a question about the tongue, about the label we hang on someone. You heard the same two words, mandaa and aakheeai, on day 247, when Guru Nanak asked why woman should be called lesser. Each time, the question turns back on the one doing the calling. Now, careful. Farid isn't saying nothing is ever wrong. His saloks are full of warnings about wasted lives and cruel deeds. You can name a wrong act clearly. What he questions is the word stamped on the whole person: bad, done, filed. The deed can be judged. That label, he says, fits no one, because there's no one without God in them. So the file never quite closes.
screen: `KHAALIK AND KHALAK, AGAIN.` · `FARID, TWO CENTURIES BEFORE KABIR.` · `AAKHEEAI — WHOM SHALL WE CALL BAD.` · `NAME THE DEED, NOT THE PERSON.` · then, large: `WHOM SHALL I CALL BAD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've quietly filed under bad. Don't pretend they've done nothing wrong. Just hold Farid's question beside them: the Creator lives in them too. Whom shall I call bad? Notice what shifts, even slightly. If nothing shifts, that's fine; just breathe with the question. Let it stay open while you rest. The bell holds the time.
Farid. Here, his salok: the Creator is in the creation and the creation in God, so whom can we call bad, when no one is without Him?
Your line: whom shall I call bad. Today, don't call anyone bad, not even in your head; if a wrong needs naming, name the deed. Day two hundred sixty.

original.note: Gurmukhi: khaalik, the Creator; from Arabic, set beside khalak, the creation.

trapdoor: what you thought: some people are just bad.
what it means: the Creator lives in every creature, so a wrong deed can be named, but no person can be written off as bad.
what a scholar hears: Salok Farid 75, Ang 1381; khaalik and khalak from the same Arabic root (kh-l-q, to create), a Sufi idea of God's presence in creation, echoed by Kabir's Prabhati hymn.
